💡 Key Takeaways
  • When I first met Stacey Abrams in 2015, she passed on to me the message that she was then passing on to anyone who’d listen: Someday soon, Georgia would be blue.
  • The following conversation has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
  • It has been revealed that ta-Nehisi Coates: My recollection of our first meeting goes back to 2015, when I was promoting Between the World and Me.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When I first met Stacey Abrams in 2015, she passed on to me the message that she was then passing on to anyone who’d listen: Someday soon, Georgia would be blue. This struck me as unlikely. But three years later Abrams ran for governor, and shocked the country by coming within two points of winning. Then two years later, when Joe Biden sealed his presidential election in 2020 with a win in Georgia, and Raphael Warnock and Jon Ossoff won Senate seats, Abrams looked prophetic. Now, Democrats have gone beyond Georgia, penetrating into the deepest reaches of the South—Mississippi, South Carolina, Texas. To understand how the GOP’s Solid South grew brittle, I could think of no better person to talk to than Abrams.

The following conversation has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

It has been revealed that ta-Nehisi Coates: My recollection of our first meeting goes back to 2015, when I was promoting Between the World and Me. You interviewed me for the book. We had a wonderful discussion. My family was actually in the audience, because, like all Black folks, I have family in Atlanta. They were so excited. I was talking to Stacey Abrams—Minority Leader Stacey Abrams. And one of the things you stated backstage was, “We’re going to make Georgia blue.” And I don’t know that I scoffed at you. I like to think I wasn’t quite that rude.

Stacey Abrams: Your eyebrow arched a bit.

According to recent reports, I confess to the eyebrow arching. And so the eyebrow arched and you made the case. Can you tell me what you saw?

I’d gone through redistricting, and one of the component pieces of redistricting, of course, is that it’s predicated on the census. The US census is a tool that is incredibly powerful and deeply inexact. It was the first time Republicans had power to draw the lines since Reconstruction. And I took a posture in my caucus, and it was this: “If you vote for their maps, I will come after your seats.” And I was not only unequivocal in saying it, I wrote it down because I didn’t want anyone to misquote me.

In order to take that posture, I had to read the maps myself. And what I saw was that Republicans were placing bets that, by drawing the lines a certain way, they were going to give themselves 124 of 180 seats. So 67% of the seats, even though they’d only won the election by 57%.

But I looked at those same maps and I’m like, In this place, in this part of Paulding County, there is a new subdivision that is predominantly Black. And in this part of Gwinnett County, there is a burgeoning Korean population that is now going into its second generation, which means a lot of those will be eligible voters. And down in South Georgia, you have third-generation migrant farm workers who are Latino, but who have decided to plant their roots here and raise their families here. When you looked at those numbers, the maps had a very different story to tell about Republican dominance: They could win for a decade. They could not win for a generation.

We tell ourselves stories about the information we get, and people repeat stories without ever reading it themselves. There are a lot of people who can quote Tom Sawyer who’ve never read the book. And so in our politics, that happens a lot, that the story that becomes popular doesn’t ever get traced back to its origin or to the original text.

Sources indicate that what I saw in Georgia is true in Louisiana, in Mississippi, in Tennessee, in Alabama, in South Carolina. We just saw it happen in North Carolina.

So when you saw this wave of redistricting happening around the country this year, did you see a similar opportunity?

Oh, absolutely. I was in Tennessee the day that they passed the maps and what stuck out for me was Raumesh Akbari, who’s the Senate minority leader, she asked to see the bill, and the Republican chair of the committee remarked, “Well, we don’t have a bill yet, but we know what it’s going to say.” They planned to vote on it even though they did not have the text of the bill.

The Republicans were moving so fast because they thought they understood what they were pulling together. Justin Pearson didn’t pick up the seat he wanted, but they were at risk of losing a seat they thought was going to be theirs because they misread the topography, but they didn’t do a deeper dive into exactly what was laying in the crevices. And that’s where opportunity for us is born.

Recent findings suggest that there are not enough Black people to win any single seat outright on their own in most legislative districts, and no statewide elections, especially post–Louisiana v. Callais, but there are coalitions that can be built. And what I saw from the very beginning was the possibility of coalition.

What I see for the South, what I think the South proved on Tuesday, is the possibility of coalition, but coalition does not happen without conflict. It does not happen without conversation, and it does not happen when we have convinced ourselves of the permanence of our second-class citizenship and our subjugation. What we saw on Tuesday was a moment where people realized that the power to improve their own lives had become so desperately thin that they had to use it or lose it. We cannot rely on that for the next two years.

In a recent development, what I hear you saying is that the last two years created an emergency. But that can’t be depended on. It can’t be “The Most Crucial Election of Our Lifetime” every two years. Desperation is not enough.

Sources indicate that it can’t be. Desperation gets you one moment. There’s a whole body of medical research on people that have heart attacks and they get saved. And what it shows is that they are exercise fiends for about six weeks and then they fall back into their patterns because it’s a normalcy bias.

It has been revealed that if we constantly feel on the edge of danger, we cannot function. And so we reorient our understanding of normal to survive. And therefore our responsibility in this moment is to look at the opportunity that was revealed on Tuesday, but not read into it that that opportunity either requires desperation or it requires this milquetoast approach, because our default is not just normalcy, but the most banal form of normalcy we can imagine.

In a recent development, I know you have some concerns about some of the narratives emerging out of the midterms. Would you talk a bit about that?

According to recent reports, I saw something on Axios that I think was well-intentioned and it essentially noted that the threats to our democracy were overblown, that our courts held, that our Congress held, that our presidency wasn’t overreaching, and that for normal people, things were fine. How have we reached the place where we think it is normal that the capital city in the United States of America is under military occupation? How is it okay that the courts held when it permits the incarceration of children in Dilley, Texas, and the kidnapping of people of color because of race and the language that they speak? There is something aggressively privileged about this idea that democracy is not in jeopardy because those who are the most protected don’t feel harm.

Sources indicate that but Tuesday was a repudiation of this idea that things are normal. You saw turnout at extraordinary levels from a cross section of communities, almost all of whom have been directly impacted by the harms of this administration. Not just the economic harms that hit everyone, but harms that were amplified and refined for their cruelty.

According to recent reports, at the same time, there’s a worry that I have that, because we won control of Congress for the patriots—and that’s how I frame it, I no longer think it’s just Democrat versus Republican, it’s patriots versus authoritarians—even though the patriots may have gained more purchase in Congress, we still have a Supreme Court that gutted the last vestiges of protection for the Voting Rights Act. We still have a Supreme Court that stripped women of their bodily autonomy. We still have a Supreme Court that has noted that protections that are afforded by DEI are somehow suspect. And when those are true, then the successes of Tuesday don’t signal that we’ve won. They signal that we have to work even harder because the harms have not dissipated, they just haven’t penetrated.

You said something a few months back that’s stuck with me—that our elections are ripe for entertainment. As a sports fan, I think it’s not a coincidence that so many sports figures are now commenting on politics because the way they appear on TV is actually quite similar to the way sports appears. You have these long campaigns, which is like your season. Then you have primaries, which are like your playoffs, and then you have this major Super Bowl that happens on Tuesday. And so, it’s an entertainment and ratings bonanza. And I think, as I recall, you were cautioning against that as a view of politics. Can you speak a little bit more about that?

Yeah. When you think about politics, if you think about elections as an event, and to extend your analogy, if the elections are the finals, if the elections are game seven, if it’s the Super Bowl, when that happens, then the day after, you go home, the game is over. But the challenge I have is that it’s not just that we treat it as a sporting event, it’s that we treat politics as though we are spectators at a sporting event. And when we look at the other party, it’s like we are spectators watching a very disciplined, seasoned team that practices in the off-season, that travels together, that plays overseas. They’re constantly engaged and we are on and off. We think of politics, again, as entertainment as opposed to the job.

How did we end up with this entertainment narrative?

According to recent reports, theodore White did this series where he examined elections 1960, 1964, 1968, 1972. And when you read it, as someone who is reading it in the 21st century, the arc of how we have viewed politics changed dramatically, specifically in 1960 with the advent of television, because the election contest between John Kennedy and Richard Nixon hinged in no small part on that televised debate. And I think for you and me and for anyone who wasn’t old enough to see it, I did not realize that it was one of the most watched programs in American history. We take for granted how many people are going to watch the debates these days, but with that first debate, it was one of the most watched programs in the world because it had never happened before. And the moment it became a television spectacle, it became entertainment because you were watching, you picked winners and losers, you picked your villain and you picked your champion.

Sources indicate that it’s human nature, we put things into these narrative arcs. As someone who writes comic books, you understand this. As someone who writes thrillers, I think about this. You create a villain, you have a protagonist, an antagonist, you have to have a storyline, you have to have complications, and when television became the medium, it added a layer and a texture to what had long been the mechanics of politics. Then you add into it the drama of Black and brown people getting to participate. And then you layer on top of that “blue state versus red state,” and the sharp division, and the attribution to entire regions of a value system and a personality based on a single day.

Sources indicate that what would it mean to remain engaged beyond elections? When I think about the conservative movement, I think about the degree to which the religious right is engaged. I think about Trump rallies. I think people were baffled by this at first—the clothes, the trucks, the boats. But what I would say is those are markers of community. They aren’t my politics. But they seem part of something larger than a particular bill or policy.

There’s a lot of talk in organizing about going for belief first, or belonging first. On the left, we are often accused of belief, that you have to be in line with all of our ideas, our values, our ideologies, but also the tactical, practical ways of exercising them, and that because we say you have to believe first, we filter out people who haven’t had time to understand or adapt or even decide what they believe. The right uses belonging. They say, “Come and be a part of us, and we’ll tell you what we are.” So you get the jersey, you get the cap, you get the red, you get to use the language, even if you haven’t decided that you actually believe all they believe, which is why you have people who are suddenly surprised that this is what happened.

We have to shift. Not to say that we don’t have beliefs, but we have to give people time to grow into those beliefs. I come at this from my time as minority leader. I had a caucus of 60 members in a chamber of 180, and my members included suburban white mothers and rural Black pastors and everything in between. We were the most racially diverse caucus. We were geographically diverse. And I had no power. I was the minority leader. My job was to help harmonize their approach. I could not lead with belief, because people were entitled to their beliefs, but my job was to bring them into belonging first because they were members of the caucus. And then my second job was to make sure that anyone who needed them to believe something had the platform to offer the tutelage.

That’s the place where I think we are failing. We don’t do the tutelage. We say, “There has been a conversation, this is now our truth. And if you don’t adopt that truth, you are somehow opposed to it,” as opposed to, “You haven’t adopted the truth because you don’t know what it means and you don’t understand it and you haven’t experienced it. Let me give you time and space to come in,” or, “You have legitimate disagreement, and maybe on this, we will not be in alignment, but your disagreement should not lead to hostility against my community.”.

The Democratic Socialists of America have attracted a lot of attention recently, but one thing they seem to do is this “belonging” piece. I can’t say I understood this before, but I was talking to someone for a story, and then mentioned the social environment. So here in New York, when people go out to canvas, afterwards, they all go out for beers. The beers are not really the point, but making people feel like they belong to something is.

Sources indicate that yeah. I mean, what they are doing is what works in most effective social movements. During the Vietnam War, one of the most effective protest waves happened at coffee shops. You brought people together around the table, they got to vent about what they were upset about, they went out and protested and then they came back together. People like being liked.

In a recent development, in terms of belief, how does one do that and not make those who are in that coalition who are particularly vulnerable feel abandoned? Obviously, I mean, this is not the only case, but I’m thinking about the tremendous amount of negative attention brought on the trans community. What do you do when the “belonging” comes in conflict with actually protecting the members of your coalition?

It has been revealed that my first position is, if you have a faith that tells you it is okay to cause harm because you feel uncomfortable, I need to understand where your faith lies. Our first responsibility is the protection of difference. And it is to say you don’t have to embrace, but you cannot lift up pitchforks. You cannot demonize, you cannot revile, you cannot scapegoat because all of those are hostile actions of cruelty that not only cause harm to the victim, they diminish your ability to learn. So the worry I have is that too often we sacrifice that education piece because it’s uncomfortable and because it requires defending those you may not be in complete alignment with, and it’s an easier thing to just jump on the bandwagon.

It has been revealed that in my caucus, when I was a minority leader, another concern I had was abortion, and I had two members who were pastors. I was not going to be able to change their ideological position and I wasn’t going to try. But I had these members walk off the floor, instead of voting, on abortion bills. And there were some who got mad and they’re like, “Oh, we should know their position.” I said, “A yes vote on this bill causes harm, and no vote is a help. Not voting is the same as a no vote. So why do you need them to make a declaration when their declaration of refusing to do harm is progress?” So there’s a complexity that we often elide because we failed to measure what harm looks like, and the path from good to harm is a lot shorter than we want to believe.

Did you work with Angie Nixon during her race?

I feel like she excited a certain element of the base in a way that we haven’t really seen before.

Industry observers note that I contributed and then I went down to Florida, actually did an event at Florida A&M University and did one at Cafe Resistance. I got to know her mama. I traveled with her some. I knew of her as a state representative. And when I decided to support her campaign, it was because she has always put the work of serving people first. She has built networks, but more importantly, she solves problems.

Industry observers note that when Florida started banning books, she started a bookstore for banned books. That kind of tactical response with strategic intention is often lacking and it has been part of how I try to operate. We’ve got people who are good at being diagnosticians and we’ve got folks who can offer prescriptions and we’ve got people who can actually administer the medicine. And we need more people who are willing to do all three. You need people who are specialists; I’m not saying you don’t, but what she has demonstrated is the capacity to do the three.

Have you heard some of the negative commentary after the election about her campaign? I’m thinking about James Carville, for instance—this notion that somehow she was a poor fit for Florida or was a bad candidate. It’s not great. Have you seen any of this?

I have. I don’t read very much of it.

In a recent development, well, I have thoughts on the fact that we keep thinking the solution to the problem is the thing that failed before. And I believe in experimentation. If you look at my history, I have never been top of mind as the solution to problems. And some of it is timing, some of it is capacity, and some of it is helping change the public imagination, but we’re never going to get what we need if we only use what we’ve always had.

I just find it interesting that she is attracting negative commentary, from certain quarters, in a way that David Jolly is not, even though they both lost and the margin wasn’t that much between the two of them. She came very, very close to winning, in a state Democrats really didn’t expect to compete in two years ago. And look, I just have to say, you are somebody who in 2018 came really, really close too. You’re both Black women. I just wonder what you make of the critique.

It has been revealed that the critique is easy because Angie Nixon is different. She’s different than what they are used to, and she is different than 250 years of expectation has led us to presume is right. I am excited about Juliana Stratton and Angela Alsobrooks and Lisa Blunt Rochester being in the US Senate. That is an extraordinary thing. Adding Angie Nixon would’ve been an amazing, amazing addition. But for pundits whose sense of success is grounded in past history, she strains the imagination.

David Jolly ran a smart race. Angie Nixon ran a smart race, and we know that because they came close to winning, but you are never entitled to victory. You are entitled to effort. And this notion that there is some magical formula for what wins in the South got completely obliterated yesterday when Scott Colom won a seat that we haven’t held since 1874. We know that what can win is a combination of a smart candidate, an invested campaign, and an electorate who sees and hears themselves in the story told.

It has been revealed that angie didn’t get that opportunity because she had a late primary and no resources. And to judge her using a metric that was never designed for her is deeply problematic. And it’s not just about her being a Black woman, it’s about how do we win an evolving electorate if all we know is to do what we’ve always done? And so my argument for the Democratic Party is that our notions of electability have to evolve with the democracy that we deserve and that we design, and it cannot be anchored to these sometimes antiquated notions that the only thing we can do is not lose as opposed to let’s try really hard to win by meeting the moment. And I think Angie Nixon did an incredible job of meeting the moment.

And what about you—do you still have ambitions for public office?

In a recent development, do you worry that some of the work you do as a kind of public political strategist (like in this interview, frankly) will conflict at all? When I think about people seeking office, they often try to say as little as possible.

Politics is a tool. It is not an identity for me. It’s a tool. And that’s different. And there are people for whom this is what they do and we need those people. This is not a disparaging comment about others, but for me, it is a tool. It is one of the ways to do the work I believe needs to be done. I think that poverty is immoral. I think it is solvable. I think it is economically inefficient. And for most of my life, the work for me has been about how do you solve this economic poverty? When I got deep in the work, I realized that we also had a moral poverty that we had to contend with, and we have this poverty of imagination. And the problem is you cannot convince people to believe that their problems can be solved if you won’t talk about them.

And in the South, silence is protective. It has been a way to nibble around the edges, but the only people who could be loud about it were the people who could afford volume. And politicians rarely can afford volume. I want things to be better and I’m not willing to forgo any tool that will make that happen. But I’m also not willing to protect my future opportunities by rejecting my current responsibilities.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon is offering early Black Friday discounts on like-newly introduced versions of its 2024 Kindles, with prices starting at $152.99 for the Paperwhite and savings of $27 to $75 across five models that include the color-screen Colorsoft and the pen-equipped Kindle Scribe. All five are a generation behind Amazon's current lineup: The manufacturer introduced redesigned Paperwhite and Colorsoft models (plus accessories) in October, with the new Paperwhite now starting at $199.99, and replaced the 2024 Scribe with a third-generation model in December 2025. As for its “like-new” label, it means these are pre-owned devices that Amazon has tested and certified to look and work like new.

The Like-Upcoming Kindle Paperwhite (16GB) is down to $152.99 from $179.99 and covers just about everything most people need for everyday reading, including enough storage for thousands of ebooks. Its seven-inch, 300ppi glare-free display is larger than the previous generation’s 6.8-inch screen, with faster page turns, an adjustable warm light, IPX8 water resistance, and up to 12 weeks of battery life. As PCMag notes in its review, it's a great option for readers who don't need color or handwriting features.

Sources indicate that the Like-Fresh Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition (32GB) is down to $190.99 from $224.99, making it just $38 more than the like-new Paperwhite (16GB). For that relatively small difference, you're doubling the storage to 32GB and getting wireless charging, an ad-free lock screen, and a front light that automatically adjusts to your surroundings—on top of the same sharp seven-inch display, IPX8 water resistance, and up to 12 weeks of battery life as the standard Paperwhite, as noted by this PCMag review.

The Like-Latest Kindle Colorsoft (16GB) is down to $220.99 from $260.99 and offers something the Paperwhite models can’t: a color E-Ink display, which makes it well suited to comics, graphic novels, illustrated books, and travel guides. Its seven-inch screen demonstrates that color content at 150ppi while keeping text at a sharp 300ppi, and you can mark passages in multiple highlight colors to keep your notes organized. That mentioned, colors are noticeably more muted than on a conventional tablet, and battery life tops out at eight weeks, compared with 12 weeks on the Paperwhite.

In a recent development, the Like-New Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition (32GB) is down to $243.99 from $287.99, making it just $23 more than the standard like-new Colorsoft. For that modest increase, you're getting twice the storage at 32GB, which is particularly useful for comics, manga, and graphic novels that take up more space than regular ebooks, along with wireless charging, an automatically adjusting front light, and an ad-free lock screen. However, as PCMag notes in its review, the color display produces more subdued tones than a conventional tablet, so the Paperwhite remains the more economical choice if you primarily read novels.

The Like-New Kindle Scribe (16GB) is down to $284.99 from $359.99, the biggest dollar discount in this roundup. Unlike the other Kindles here, it's built for reading and writing, with a 10.2-inch, 300ppi glare-free display and a Premium Pen with an eraser and shortcut button—making it the most versatile option for readers who want an e-reader that doubles as a digital notebook.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Industry observers note that black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

Industry observers note that yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

Recent findings suggest that AGT regularly draws claims online, with people alleging that it's scripted or faking parts of its programming. This latest claim from Reddit comes from someone who allegedly worked on the set and took glitch with how one contestant's story was edited in the episode. Take a read:.

I worked on America's Got Talent's 7th season and I never watched the show before working on it. I spent 4 days working, interviewing talented people with a camera crew and producer. It's not uncommon for reality TV show subjects to complain about receiving unflattering or dishonest edits. Over the years, stars have alleged that producers can get the response they want out of them and then edit the footage to make it appear they remarked something entirely different from what they meant. If AGT actually engaged in this, it wouldn't be different from claims against many other shows on the 2026 TV schedule. Regardless, this should be a gentle reminder for viewers not to believe everything they see.

The thread also revealed someone who was pretty upset with Bar Rescue after the show allegedly "ruined" one of his favorite locales. On that note, per the aforementioned user, his go-to bar didn't even need to be rescued:.

Sources indicate that this bar was packed ALL THE TIME. You drive by at 3 PM on a Tuesday, packed. 2 PM on a Sunday, packed. On more than one occasion, we had gone to the bar on a Friday or Saturday to find no place to sit because it was so full. They even bought the space next to them and knocked out a wall to make more room...Then we heard that Bar Rescue was coming. We wondered why they would need to 'rescue' this bar that was always full of people. But we got excited to see our bar on TV.

It has been revealed that from there, the writer claimed the bar's owners removed all the furniture and revamped the menu with new cocktails. His wife apparently stood in line to attend the reopening and was instructed before entering that she could only order the signature cocktail.

As mentioned, attendees were allegedly told they could only purchase cocktails, which made it seem like the show's producers decided that would be the story before filming ever began. In the end, the "rescue" ended up ruining the bar, at least in this person's opinion:.

People stopped going. Last time I went, it was a Friday night, and there were like 6 other people in the place. The bar ended up moving locations, and now I don't have a neighborhood place anymore. Fuck Bar Rescue.

Ocarina of Time for Switch 2 released on November 5, and Circana's reporting period ended on November 7, so the achievement was actually accomplished in just two days, not even a full week. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_xMM7L2XoMc Ocarina of Time's physical edition, which includes a cartridge, sells for $70, compared to $60 for its digital counterpart. Ocarina of Time's remake for Switch 2 sold more than 5 million copies over its first four days globally. The latest sales data for GTA 6 pre-purchases show that the game has passed 16 million units sold worldwide.

In a recent development, netflix’s dark-comedy anthology series Beef promptly captured viewers’ attention when its first season premiered on April 6, 2023. Now, less than a year after the second season finished airing, there’s an enhancement on the possibility of a third season of Beef.

The tragicomedy from showrunner Lee Sung Jin made a strong impression with its sharp humor and memorable storytelling, leaving fans eager to see what would come next. After all, it was rare to have a TV series where the biggest questions seemed to be: what if we followed people so adamant about destroying each other and everyone around them? Would that be entertaining?

Sources indicate that as it turned out, the answer was a resounding yes. The first season was well received, with 98% of critics' reviews on Rotten Tomatoes positive. Polygon’s take on the first season called it a “cataclysmic spiral of existential despair and self-destruction” and praised stars Steven Yeun and Ali Wong for their electric chemistry as bitter rivals, Danny Cho and Amy Lau.

Industry observers note that the second season moved on from Yeun and Wong, though both remained executive producers. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, say what you will about the "Batman" movies of the 1990s, there's no denying that they brought some truly massive star power to the screen. Even "Batman and Robin," often derided as the worst film of the entire franchise, was loaded with A-list actors, including Arnold Schwarzenegger, Uma Thurman, Alicia Silverstone, and a cameo appearance by the rapper Coolio. It was 1995's "Batman Forever," though, that gave the series what was arguably its biggest casting coup, when director Joel Schumacher cast Jim Carrey as the Riddler.

At the time, Carrey was experiencing a meteoric rise thanks to the success of "Ace Ventura: Pet Detective" and "Dumb and Dumber," which both released in 1994 and propelled him to the role of one of Hollywood's most prominent comedic actors. Looking back, putting him opposite Schumacher's campier Caped Crusader seems like a natural fit. Initially, however, Schumacher thought Carrey was simply too young to play the part. As revealed in a 1994 interview with "Comics Scene," the director only changed his mind when he saw Carrey bring another comic book to life on the big scree. As Carrey told the magazine, Schumacher "thought I was a little too young. Then, when he saw the trailer for 'The Mask,' he changed his mind.".

While it went through some significant changes on its way to becoming a film — mostly to tone down the violence that made director Chuck Russell initially think of it as a horror movie and add in way more swing dancing — "The Mask" started out as a comic book by writer John Arcudi and artist Doug Mahnke. Carrey, whose over-the-top delivery and exaggerated impressions made him a breakout star on the sketch comedy show "In Living Color," was the perfect fit for the cartoonish, chaotic madman that emerged when the power of the trickster god Loki wound up in the hands of a relatively lovable loser.

In a recent development, although he allegedly had a much longer cut of the film that skewed darker and more serious than the final result, Schumacher's take on Batman was heavily influenced by the 1960s TV show, so it makes sense that he'd look for a comic actor to play the Riddler. Long before the Riddler was the dark and murderous villain of "The Batman," he was one of the Dark Knight's sillier foes. Frank Gorshin, who played the Riddler to perfection on that show, was a well-known comedian and impressionist himself, and before Carrey's casting, Robin Williams was considered to be a favorite for the part. Seeing Carrey pull off the menacing silliness of "The Mask" and make that film a huge hit likely did a lot to sell Schumacher on giving Carrey a chance — and the fact that Carrey did it while wearing a lot of green probably didn't hurt either.

As for how it worked out, well, Carrey's performance as Edward Nygma in "Batman Forever" was, to put it charitably, a lot. The Riddler was undoubtedly annoying on purpose, but Carrey into being straight-up grating. Even his co-star thought so, with Tommy Lee Jones (who played Two-Face in the film) famously telling him "I cannot sanction your buffoonery" when they met.

That mentioned, there are some really great parts of his performance, too. While the Riddler was way over the top, the way Carrey plays Edward Nygma as an obsessive fanboy of Val Kilmer's Bruce Wayne, including a scene where he dresses like Wayne down to the glasses while showing off his mind-controlling invention, is actually really solid. It's also the kind of subtle — well, subtle for Carrey, at least — touch that only really worked because of Carrey's youth.

Recent findings suggest that ubisoft recently hired games industry veteran Christoph Hartmann to become the general manager of Creative House 2. In a new interview, Hartmann talked about his hopes for the unit, saying his dream would be for it to become "like the A24 of video games." He told Variety that what he means by this is that Creative House 2 can be like A24 in that it can make games that are both critically and commercially successful. A24's biggest hit ever was this year's Backrooms, which made more than $400 million worldwide against a reported budget of $10 million and was received positively by fans and critics. Some of A24's other recent significant critical and commercial hits have included Marty Supreme ($192 million), Everything Everywhere All at Once ($148 million), The Drama ($135 million), and Civil War ($127 million). Jesse Plemons in A24's Civil War. Saying Ubisoft's Creative House 2 could aim for what A24 is doing is certainly an ambitious goal, and it's not the first time that Hartmann has made such a bold claim about what he's working on. When he was at Amazon, Hartmann said his objective was to help Amazon become “the Disney of the future,” with gaming standing alongside TV, film, music, and retail. Creative House 2 covers franchises like The Division, Ghost Recon, Splinter Cell, and March of Giants (which Ubisoft bought from Hartmann's previous firm, Amazon). "Hartmann’s role is to oversee strategic direction and development of the studios and brands under Creative House 2," Ubisoft said. Hartmann told Variety that he wants Creative House 2 to "definitely not" be a place that only makes shooter games. "I want us to be a label which really looks after the core gamer. And what I mean by that, it’s almost easier to describe what we’re not going to do. So I’m not going to do a racing game. I’m not going to do sports. I’m not going to do a casual kids title. But could we do an RPG one day? Could we do MMO? Could I maybe do even a strategy game? Sure, it’s all coming down to the right talent," he said. Hartmann also discussed why he left Amazon, saying the company is focused on the AI buildout right now and "games just can't be their prime focus right now." Prior to Amazon, Hartmann worked at 2K for decades. Ubisoft restructured its business around the Creative House model after taking investment from Tencent to secure the company's financial future. Us also confirmed that Gallagher is the subject of an Apprehended Violence Application that was filed on behalf of Gael in New South Wales.

“I’m not claiming I was perfect. I wasn’t. Cameron remained largely tight-lipped before Tuesday’s podcast, where she answered burning questions about her life now.

Keep scrolling for the biggest revelations:.

“So there is a scene where we hug and we’re hugging on the stairs and he kisses me on the neck. The pair got back together when Cameron made an appearance in season 10.

In a recent development, cameron recalled confiding in her mother, adding, “What I learned and what I was told multiple times [by Nathan] is you’re not allowed to speak about your relationship to other people. … We had another really big fight and things had escalated and he’d got on the drink. I was running around Sydney very pregnant, having just finished a full day at work. … I called my best friend and I noted, ‘Hey, can you just stay on the phone with me? Nathan’s upset with me at the moment. Can you please just stay on the phone to me?’ And he jumped out of the car. The moving car. So he opened the door, I slammed the brakes and he jumped out.”.

Recent findings suggest that she continued: ”The way that I was treated, I would be told to shut the f*** up, I’d be called a bitch, a s***, and all these horrible things. There were multiple times when I was like ‘No no no, this cannot continue because my son cannot grow up thinking that this is how you speak to women.'”.

After giving birth to son Kayden, Cameron was asked to move to Croatia while Gallagher filmed Below Deck Med.

“Obviously, I didn’t think it was a good idea to go [to Croatia]. In a perfect world and with a supportive partner, I would 100 percent say, ‘Yep, we can do this, no problem.’ But obviously the situation wasn’t that,” she noted. “And DCJ, which is essentially Child Protective Services, had gotten involved.”.

Cameron recalled trying to get help. “The social worker deemed the situation to be unsafe,” she recalled. “I had even gotten onto the phone to one of the producers, and I couldn’t tell him everything. But I was just saying, ‘Look, I’m in a really bad situation and I don’t think it’s a good idea if I go [to Croatia].'”.

She continued: “It felt as though he was very worried about who I spoke to or who I was around when he wasn’t around. So it did feel like there was this element of control that he would lose over me if I wasn’t in the same country as him.”.

While watching season 11 back, Cameron wasn’t thrilled to serve as the “scapegoat” for Gallagher, sharing, “It was kind of like he was not treating everyone on the boat quite so nicely and the excuse was he was getting a hard time at home, when we were just all getting a hard time.”.

Cameron ultimately had to find a way to get her friend to Croatia after Gallagher allegedly isolated her.

“They did offer me to have someone there. They remarked we will pay for a flight for someone to come and help you [production]. And in discussions with Nathan about me coming there, I was told that I couldn’t have any one of my family or my friends come because he has to feel comfortable also. My options were his sister or his mom,” she noted. “I had to essentially devise this thing with my best friend. … She can’t take too much time off work so I said, ‘OK, how about I get there and then I say that I can’t do it on my own and then maybe ask him in front of people that maybe I need a little bit of help. Cameron tried to alert a producer to her complications, to which Gallagher responded by “crying.”.

Recent findings suggest that “He said, ‘I’m so sad that I made her feel this way.’ And I just sat there in absolute shock and awe,” she recalled. “This was the first time he had ever cried or ever demonstrated any remorse to my sadness or to my hurt. Following a tense day, Cameron claimed Gallagher was “angry” she spent time with her family.

And obviously in this scenario that made him see red and that just escalated things so much more.”.

Sources indicate that she continued: “When I was in the bathroom and he had his hands around my neck and attempted to lift, my son was in my arms. At that moment, all I could think of was, if I fall, so does he. So in that moment I step up and do anything I could and thank God there’s a toilet behind me. That’s probably the biggest part that I’m like from that moment, I should have known there’s no return.”.

Cameron remarked she was worried she wouldn’t survive the harrowing moment.

Industry observers note that “There was a moment when he had me pinned down and he was striking me on the jaw… I actually sat there and I asked if he was going to kill me. There was a moment where I actually asked that question. The reason I say this is because if things had not gotten that bad, I would never have gotten out. That’s the scary thing. Ring's Upcoming $250 Indoor Camera Drone Sounds Terrifying

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (799 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that ring made its name with its smart doorbells with built-in cameras, and now sells more indoor cameras than any other company, capturing more than 40% of the market.
  • Recent findings suggest that the drone camera is one of two products in the tech giant's new Ring Robotics line, alongside a "rover cam" that looks kind of like the canister of a vacuum cleaner attached to an iPad.
  • In a recent development, the drone camera records 2K video and has a 148-degree field of view and the ability to rotate 360 degrees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that ring made its name with its smart doorbells with built-in cameras, and now sells more indoor cameras than any other company, capturing more than 40% of the market. When you've already moved tens of millions of devices (enough to raise serious concerns about their use as part of the surveillance state), you always need to keep innovating, and today, the company revealed a product it has been working on for a decade: an indoor camera drone powered by artificial intelligence. I got a chance to check it out during a media event yesterday, and I can report that, as harbingers of our dystopian future go, it is only mildly terrifying.

Recent findings suggest that the drone camera is one of two products in the tech giant's new Ring Robotics line, alongside a "rover cam" that looks kind of like the canister of a vacuum cleaner attached to an iPad. While the Ring Rover Cam is priced at $999.99 and targeted at businesses, the Ring Drone Cam is a much more affordable $249.99, reasonable enough that it will appeal to consumers looking for another way to keep (robot) eyes on their stuff.

In a recent development, the drone camera records 2K video and has a 148-degree field of view and the ability to rotate 360 degrees. It works with existing Ring cameras, doorbells, sensors, and alarms, as well as the Alexa Home Map. It has a flight time of eight minutes, and once it returns to its base station, it takes around an hour to fully recharge (eight minutes on the dock will give it one minute in the air).

As Ring founder Jamie Siminoff explained during the preview event, the firm has been trying to build a workable camera drone for around a decade, but couldn't overcome certain design challenges until the advancement of AI models that allow the device to handle most of the computing—from route programming to threat detection—via the cloud, so the drones can be smaller and lighter.

According to Ring, when setting up the Ring Drone Cam, you carry it around your house, allowing it to map the interior. It will "intelligently identify rooms and suggest patrol points: spots worth extra attention." When sent out on "patrol," the drone's AI pilot will travel between hotspots, sensing and avoiding furniture and other obstacles along the way.The Ring Drone Cam works with other Ring cameras, so if an alert is triggered somewhere in your home—say, a window opening unexpectedly—the drone will take off to investigate. It has a built-in security light that will make its presence known, so it can also act as a deterrent, though the screaming sound of its spinning propellers will accomplish that just as well.

According to Ring, the drone camera can deliver peace of mind whether you're home or away, and admittedly I do like the idea of being able to check on my pets or make sure no pipes have burst while I'm at work or on vacation (though admittedly you can get the same sort of monitoring without involving an AI device that looks like a mini version of the flying robots from The Terminator).

Recent findings suggest that I admit that the Ring Drone Cam seems pretty cool, provided I don't think about it too much. I don't know that I really feel the need to have every inch of my home covered in security cameras, but I do like the idea that the drone could, for example, go to check out what's going on if one of my smoke alarms' temperature sensors reports that one spot in the house is all of a sudden hotter than it should be.

But there's something slightly unsettling to me about the idea of a robot patrolling my home while I sleep. Yes, I know that there are privacy and security features in place—Ring says the videos its robots capture are protected by its "strongest default encryption yet"—but it's also yet one more example of how comfortable we've all gotten with cameras being absolutely everywhere, to the point that people think nothing of putting them all over their homes. (This is probably why I don't own a robot vacuum.) And it doesn't help that the drone sounds absolutely terrifying, which Ring claims is by design: "If someone’s there who shouldn’t be, a flying drone overhead...makes it clear they’ve been spotted. [The] devices are built to deter, not just monitor." True enough, but there's also no getting around the fact that drone propellers are unavoidably loud, and the sound of the Ring Drone Cam reminds me of nothing more than the screeching violins in a horror movie. (Note that the drone we were shown was white, but the final version sold will be dark grey.).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Following a lengthy casting process that, at times, felt like it might never come to an end, Robert Pattinson has officially been cast as James Bond.
  • According to recent reports, pattinson's casting as Bond breaks a 60-year tradition of relative unknowns taking on the role.
  • As such, Pattinson's age is surely of little consequence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Following a lengthy casting process that, at times, felt like it might never come to an end, Robert Pattinson has officially been cast as James Bond. The director of the upcoming 26th Bond installment, Denis Villeneuve, and the latest custodian of the 007 franchise, Amazon MGM, have opted for one of the most consistently interesting actors working today, and it will be fascinating to see what the "Primetime" star does as England's greatest spy.

According to recent reports, pattinson's casting as Bond breaks a 60-year tradition of relative unknowns taking on the role. The British actor is one of the biggest stars in the world — which, again, means Amazon MGM shouldn't have to worry too much about box office profits. But he's also one of the most exciting actors of his generation and has been delivering fascinating performances ever since he joined the Safdie Brothers for 2017's "Good Time.".

As such, Pattinson's age is surely of little consequence. We know the man can deliver, and everyone should be looking forward to seeing what choices he makes in a role he's described as a "dream come true." But with Amazon MGM likely eyeing a 2028 release date for Pattinson's 007 debut, we've got plenty of time to kill. So, why not take a look at how he measures up to the other Bond actors in terms of age? Here are all the James Bond actors' ages in their first and last 007 movies.

In 1962, "Dr. No kicked off cinema's most enduring franchise," introducing audiences to a rugged young Scotsman by the name of Sean Connery. The actor was born on August 25, 1930, which means he was 31 when filming on "Dr. No" got underway in January 1962. By the time the movie hit theaters in October of that year, he was 32.

Recent findings suggest that director Terrence Young's urbane manner helped mold Connery's rough-around-the edges Bond into the legendary cinematic figure we remember today. By the time he made his last appearance in the tux for 1971's "Diamonds are Forever," however, he needed no help whatsoever. Filming began in April 1971 when Connery was 40. The film debuted in December of that year, by which point the actor — who passed away in 2020 — was 41, the same age Robert Pattinson will likely be by the time his Bond movie starts shooting. A 52-year-old Connery returned for an unofficial Bond entry in 1983's "Never Say Never Again.".

Industry observers note that george Lazenby is the only James Bond actor to only appear in the role once. Thankfully, his sole outing as 007 was one of the best Bond movies ever made. 1969's "On Her Majesty's Secret Service" was a brilliant installment in the franchise and is Christopher Nolan's favorite Bond film. Considering Lazenby was following in Sean Connery's footsteps, that's a pretty impressive accomplishment.

According to recent reports, born on September 5, 1939, the Australian model-turned-actor was 29 when filming on "On Her Majesty's Secret Service" began in October 1968. By the time the film debuted in December 1969, Lazenby had turned 30. That was it for the Aussie star, who's still going strong today at the age of 87. "On Her Majesty's Secret Service" was his first and only Bond outing, and Lazenby remains the youngest ever actor to play the role.

After Sean Connery's brief return as James Bond in "Diamonds Are Forever" Roger Moore donned the tux for 1973's "Live and Let Die." The British actor was born on October 14, 1927. Almost exactly 45 years later, his first Bond outing began shooting on October 13, 1972, making him 44 when production started and 45 by the time the movie debuted in June 1973.

That made him older than both Connery and George Lazenby, regardless of whether we're talking their first or last 007 movie. Today, he's still the oldest actor ever cast as James Bond.

Recent findings suggest that moore retired from the Bond saga with his seventh appearance in the role. He was 57 when "A View to a Kill" bowed in May 1985, and all too aware of his age. The actor told Entertainment Weekly: "I became very conscious that I was getting long in the tooth to play the great lover." More than 40 years later, Moore remains the oldest actor to ever portray Bond.

It has been revealed that next to George Lazenby, Timothy Dalton is surely the most underrated of all the James Bond actors. He brought a darkness to the character long before Daniel Craig's tortured spy debuted, and his interpretation of Bond remains one of the most interesting in the series' history.

In a recent development, the actor was born in Wales on March 21, 1946, making him 40 years old when filming got underway on 1987's "The Living Daylights." When the film opened in July 1987 in the United States, Dalton was 41. He only portrayed Bond in one other film, 1989's "Licence to Kill," and was 42 when filming commenced in July 1988. The movie hit theaters in July 1989, by which time he was 43. Dalton almost played Bond again in 1995's "GoldenEye," but the film took some time to come together and when it did, former Bond custodians EON Productions had found someone new.

After Timothy Dalton's brief James Bond tenure came to an end, EON tapped a dashing young Irishman by the name of Pierce Brosnan to be his successor. 1995's "GoldenEye" is a pretty silly movie viewed in retrospect, but it will remain forever legendary for capturing the imagination of a whole newly introduced generation of Bond fans, who rapidly became further enraptured by the video game tie-in.

Brosnan was born May 16, 1953, making him 41 when "GoldenEye" filming began in January 1995. The film bowed in theaters in November of that year, by which time he had turned 42 — just a year younger than Dalton in his final Bond performance.

Seven years later, Brosnan made his fourth and final appearance as 007 in "Die Another Day," which makes "GoldenEye" look like a work of pure artistic genius in comparison. Brosnan's now infamous final turn as 007 (it's the worst Bond film according to IMDb) started shooting in January 2002, at which point the actor was 48. When it hit theaters in November of that year he'd turned 49 and was well and truly done with the Bond franchise.

Recent findings suggest that daniel Craig will always be in contention for the title of best James Bond simply because he starred in the best James Bond movie ever made: 2006's "Casino Royale." Craig was born on March 2, 1968, and was 37 when filming began in January of 2006. That makes him the third youngest Bond to be cast in the role. He was 38 when "Casino Royale" arrived in theaters in November 2006.

According to recent reports, sadly, Craig's Bond tenure was characterized by diminishing returns and things went badly awry with 2021's "No Time to Die." Craig had clearly had enough by that point, too. The actor was 51 when filming started in April 2019, and 53 when the film was released in October 2021. It marked his fifth and final time playing Bond, and saw him become the second-oldest actor to ever portray the character after Roger Moore.

It has been revealed that so, we come to the man himself. Robert Pattinson is now officially set to debut as James Bond in Denis Villeneuve's upcoming film. Just what the director has planned remains a mystery at this point, but casting Pattinson is a great start.

According to recent reports, the actor beat out other finalists including Josh O'Connor, Jack Lowden, and Nicholas Hoult, to take the coveted role as England's greatest spy. Interestingly enough, he was the oldest of the bunch. The British actor was born on May 13 1986, making him 40 years old at the time he was cast as 007. The movie will likely start shooting in early 2027, so he will either be 40 or 41 at the time of filming. That puts Pattinson in the middle of the pack in terms of every Bond actor's age at the time of their casting.

Bond fans have reacted to Pattinson's casting with a mix of excitement and trepidation at what many see as a fairly safe choice. Those who've been following his career, however, should have no doubt he'll deliver in his Bond debut.

Christopher Nolan Helped Rescue Theaters — Now He Could Save Physical Media

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (594 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Whether or not you're a fan of the films of Christopher Nolan, there's a lot to appreciate about him, especially for cinephiles.
  • According to recent reports, this influential power of Nolan's may now be extending to the cause of physical media.
  • While this could be a mere one-off incident, it's more likely Best Buy is dipping its toes back into the water of selling movies again.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Whether or not you're a fan of the films of Christopher Nolan, there's a lot to appreciate about him, especially for cinephiles. Chief among his virtues is his dedication to celluloid itself, as he's been instrumental in helping physical film stay alive, both for shooting and exhibiting features. The rise of Premium Large Format screens can be directly linked to his embrace of IMAX, too. Both of these facts have heavily contributed to the rescue of movie theatergoing, which seemed inevitably doomed in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic. Thanks to Nolan setting an example and others in the industry following his lead, we have a newly robust theatrical exhibition landscape which only continues to improve.

According to recent reports, this influential power of Nolan's may now be extending to the cause of physical media. The filmmaker has long been a proponent of films being made available for purchase on disc. In fact, he said as much in November 2023, which coincidentally was just a month after the retail giant Best Buy publicly revealed it would be discontinuing the sale of physical media movies in its online and physical stores. Cut to this week, where it appears this tide may be turning: Employees and fans have shared that Best Buy will be selling physical copies of Nolan's "The Odyssey" in its stores, marking the first time since 2023 that the company has reneged on its stance.

While this could be a mere one-off incident, it's more likely Best Buy is dipping its toes back into the water of selling movies again. If this move is successful, it would mean that Nolan has once again helped save films and film culture from the scourge of corporations and the tech industry trying to fix something that wasn't broken.

Recent findings suggest that on paper, it makes all the sense in the world for Best Buy to make "The Odyssey" 4K UHDs available for purchase. The film is one of the biggest hits of 2026, and could be on its way to some nominations (if not wins) at the Academy Awards. Other competitors like Walmart still sell physical media in their locations, and have never stopped. It's also the Christmas shopping season, and movies on disc are a great holiday gift for many.

Recent findings suggest that for now, it seems Best Buy will only be selling the 4K version of "The Odyssey" — the Premium Giftset edition and other formats like a Steelbook appear to be sold via online retailers only. Yet while the retailer may not be catering to hardcore physical media collectors as it used to during its heyday, Best Buy reinstating the sale of physical movies, even on a limited basis for now, is a massive deal.

What's undeniable is how this choice on the part of the company is as good an indicator as any that the market for physical media is alive and well. Sure, most average folks have been trained to utilize streaming services as their primary source of entertainment, yet the recent complications that have cropped up with digital-only services (particularly in the gaming world) have made even casual disc buyers more interested in rebuilding their collections. While the physical media market has a long way to go to recapture its former glory (and may never reach those heights again), it's so wonderful to see folks like Nolan put their weight behind keeping discs alive. How fitting that "The Odyssey" is the release where physical media at Best Buy finally returns in a significant way.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, spinning off of a popular web series, Netflix's Minimum Wage is presently in the middle of a 28-episode first-season run. If that sounds like a lot of episodes for a show in 2026, keep in mind that they're generally less than 15 minutes each, which is perfect for your overloaded to-watch list—especially when they go down so easily. This cringe workplace mockumentary follows the crew of teenagers running a failing pizza place and making (you guessed it) minimum wage; they're under enormous pressure from their boss (Randall Park) to save the business and their one dumb source of income.

It has been revealed that the punchy episodes will leave you plenty of time to explore other streaming shows dealing with the utter ridiculousness of the modern workplace. Here are 10 to get you started.

It has been revealed that workplace comedies usually revolve around white-collar office environments (The Mary Tyler Moore Show, 30 Rock, Parks and Recreation, etc.). Like Minimum Wage, Superstore instead follows the staff of Cloud 9, a generic big-box retailer. The show’s deep bench and diverse cast are largely focused on the jokes, but much of that comedy involves the relatable situation of working a job that demands commitment and a smiley attitude in the face of both entitled customers and obnoxious bosses. It's a different venue and age bracket, but a nutty workplace is a nutty workplace. Stream Superstore on Hulu and Peacock.

We're moving away from the workplace and aging things up a bit, but no worries: the name is a little ironic given that the codependent, co-habitating twenty-somethings of the title are hardly mature. Five friends are cohabiting in the childhood home of Samir (Malik Elassal), and dealing with the uniquely Gen-Z humiliations around dating, work, and even health insurance. Only one member of the group has an actual reasonably good job, while career paths for the others include being a temp, waiter, and a part-time ballet instructor. Stream Adults on Hulu.

This offbeat workplace comedy kicks off with a fabulous premise: Jeong Bok-dong (Kim Byung-chul) was a high-level director in a major corporation until one bad meeting saw him demoted. To president! ...of the company's failing Pegasus Mart offshoot. Bok-dong makes it his mission to get revenge by bankrupting the store, hiring eccentrics to execute eccentric, entirely whackadoo plans and accidentally getting Pegasus noticed by customers, who rapidly make it more popular than ever. Think The Producers, but in retail. Stream Pegasus Market on Tubi.

It might sound a little (or a lot) niche, but we’ve seen enough headlines about the working conditions at many video game production houses to understand why a workplace comedy set against such a backdrop would make for a dark and juicy comedy. Charlotte Nicdao and Rob McElhenney are the leads, playing a brilliant workaholic and an unsociable egomaniac, respectively, and the chemistry between them gives the show more than enough spark. There's also a four-episode spin-off called Side Quest. Stream Mythic Quest.

Recent findings suggest that A half-hour comedy-drama with an emphasis on the comedy, Gentefied follows three Mexican-American cousins who have built lives in Los Angeles, only to be faced with a newly introduced challenge: the looming gentrification of the neighborhood they helped to build via their family's taco shop. Gentefied has a baked-in sense of place and culture and a lot of heart; the second season is even better than the first. Stream Gentefied on Netflix.

According to recent reports, perhaps there's a bit of counter-programming in this dramedy about a couple of scrappy Newly introduced York City outsiders, but there's a fundamental goofiness to this show about a couple of nice guys who are great at getting themselves into trouble, and equally good at talking themselves out of it. Bryan Greenberg plays Ben Epstein, a quiet guy with any number of substantial ideas, while Victor Rasuk plays the outgoing, often shameless Cam Calderon; together they manage a startup clothing business with the benefits of neither money nor experience, amiably hustling their way to success, maybe. Stream How to Make It in America on HBO Max and Netflix.

Debuting at the beginning of the Obama administration before getting a surprise revival just a couple of years ago, Party Down is an acclaimed cult sitcom for the ages—lots of laughs, low ratings, and always worth rediscovering. A group of six (or so) struggling LA actors and writers work as cater waiters for a fancy company, with every episode into a fresh and wildly absurd situation, even as their aspirations far outstrip their actual lives. Stream Party Down on Prime Video and Netflix.

A legitimate sitcom that just happens to be set in Northern Ireland during the violent Troubles of the 1990s, when clashes between nationalists and unionists frequently resulted in violence. It’s a fascinating contrast, brought to life by a writer and creator (Lisa McGee) who lived it. It’s also laugh-out-loud funny—though it doesn’t make any allowances for audiences unaccustomed to Irish accents, so don’t feel bad if you need subtitles until you get the hang of it. Erin, Orla, Clare, and Michelle are joined by James, the only male student at their Catholic girls' school, dealing with normal growing-up stuff in absurd times. This world is a far cry from that of Minimum Wage, but Lisa McGee's sense of the absurd connects both demonstrates—if the setting is a bit more dramatic, the comedy is just as wonderfully silly. Stream Derry Girls on Netflix.

Recent findings suggest that not a comedy! But about as good an indication of where we are in the modern global workplace as you're likely to find. Hyuk‑jun is a young guy saddled with debt who signs on for some part-time work at a job agency...at 50x the going rate, no less (should've been a red flag). Each upcoming assignment places him in new and increasingly horrific situations, with increasingly arbitrary-seeming rules. But, hey, in 2026, it's a living. Stream Dead-End Job on Netflix.

It's an office (obviously) and not a pizza joint, but the point here is kinda that white-collar jobs in the 21st century can be at least as soul-killing as working customer service. The Office inherited some of the finer tropes of the workplace comedy (mostly involving tossing together a group of weirdos overly invested in their jobs) while also launching a million mockumentary-style shows, running for nine seasons, and becoming one of the most popular shows of its era. Stream The Office on Peacock.

Jet Li And Morgan Freeman's Forgotten Martial Arts Movie Is Worth Revisiting

  • Recent findings suggest that "Unleashed" has everything you might want from a Saturday afternoon matinee.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Louis Leterrier's 2005 action flick "Unleashed," written by Luc Besson, is a fun, intense, somewhat strange vehicle for martial arts superstar Jet Li. In the film, Li plays Danny, a vicious bodyguard for a Glasgow gangster named Bart (Bob Hoskins). Bart has mentally conditioned Danny to remain calm and obedient when he is wearing a metal collar, but he turns feral and deadly when Bart takes the collar off. Danny is a "dog" and, occasionally, he is literally unleashed.

Meanwhile, Morgan Freeman co-stars as Sam, a blind pianist who takes Danny into his home after he gets separated from Bart during a "dogfighting" tournament. Sam and his stepdaughter Victoria (Kerry Condon) then raise Danny to be more gentle and humane and, in time, are able to remove his collar without Danny becoming violent. Because of this, Danny begins to remember his past and develops an interest in music, finding his humanity again. Naturally, though, Bart eventually re-emerges in Danny's life, leaving him torn between his newfound family and the violence he was conditioned to live in.

Recent findings suggest that "Unleashed" has everything you might want from a Saturday afternoon matinee. It has recognizable movie stars, it sports a pretty good performance by Li, and it features works by the always reliable Freeman and Hoskins, as well as the somewhat under-appreciated Condon. There's a reason /Film previously listed it as an underrated martial arts movie, as well as one of Li's top 10 best movies in general.

The film also doesn't forget that it has to be at least 40% martial arts scenes to justify casting Li, with legendary martial arts choreographer Yuen Woo-Ping providing its fight choreography. It was hardly a hit, but "Unleashed" is certainly worth tracking down.

Sources indicate that it's worth pausing to note that "Unleashed," aesthetically speaking, is very much a product of its time. Pierre Morel's cinematography has the green-tint and artificially enhanced grain that was so in vogue in the 2000s (along with several harshly-lit scenes), while the film is edited by Nicolas Trembasiewicz in a haphazard and swift style that will make your head spin. To be sure, "Unleashed" very much bears a distinctly mid-'00s action aesthetic.

Sources indicate that additionally, the film's score was provided by trip hop collective Massive Attack and produced by the RZA. Its soundtrack was originally released under the title "Danny the Dog," and it mostly consists of electronic and/or ambient beats. This only further dates "Unleashed," adding to what one might call its "2000s edgelord" design.

According to recent reports, but in spite of this, "Unleashed" remains grounded thanks to Jet Li's amazing performance and Morgan Freeman's gentle confidence. Kerry Condon also brings a childlike innocence to the movie as Victoria, giving Danny someone to relate to. Condon was in her early 20s when "Unleashed" was made, but the film gives her braces and a youthful demeanor, creating the impression that her character might be a high schooler.

Sources indicate that above it all, "Unleashed" is an effective melodrama. When Danny begins to remember his past late in the film, he recalls the deep tragedy of his upbringing and the dark circumstances that led him into the thrall of the evil Bart to begin with. Indeed, Bob Hoskins is so good at playing heavies and gangsters that he infuses "Unleashed" with a good amount of menace. (Bart is not a good guy by any stretch of the imagination.).

Critics generally liked "Unleashed," with the larger critical consensus being that "Unleashed" is "good enough." Many of the film's reviews similarly cite its performances and humanity as key elements that offsets its fighting and violence.

Case in point: Roger Ebert gave the movie three stars out of four, writing that its story was familiar and that it "could have made a laughable movie. That it works is because of the performances of Jet Li and Bob Hoskins, who plays his master." He added:.

Sources indicate that "The film is ingenious in its construction. It has all the martial arts action any Jet Li fan could possibly desire, choreographed by Yeun Woo-ping, who is the Gerald Arpino of kung-fu and creates improbable but delightful ballets of chops and socks, leaps and twists and kicks and improvisations. Everything happens in a denatured sepia tone that is not black and white nor quite color, but a palette drained of cheer and pressing down like a foggy day.".

(Gerald Arpino, for those unfamiliar with the name, was a famed ballet dancer and choreographer who was head of the Joffrey Ballet for decades.).

Industry observers note that ebert is spot-on with his observation about the denatured sepia of "Unleashed." Everything does feel depressive as a result. When it comes to actioners like this, though, "better than average" can actually serve as high praise. Unlike many other action films, you might actually remember this one.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that on more than one occasion, the idea of Timothée Chalamet as the last male movie star has been a debate here at the office, usually ending in uneasy agreement: He is one of very few left, maybe the only one of his generation.
  • All of which is why we are thrilled to have Chalamet on our cover as he sets out to open the final, breathtaking installment of Denis Villeneuve’s Dune trilogy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the history of actors appearing in Vanity Fair goes back about as far as the movies themselves. Making a studio-orchestrated, Edward Steichen–captured debut in the pages of this magazine was a milestone in the careers of Gary Cooper, Gloria Swanson, Anna May Wong, and dozens of others, many of whom never made it to Technicolor.

Sources indicate that on more than one occasion, the idea of Timothée Chalamet as the last male movie star has been a debate here at the office, usually ending in uneasy agreement: He is one of very few left, maybe the only one of his generation. He is in the tradition of Marlon Brando and Leonardo DiCaprio in that his knowability runs inverse to his fame. Like other endangered species, his extreme rarity makes him celebrated and isolated in equal measure. And with each of these stars, one rule usually holds true: The bigger they get, the less they open their mouth.

All of which is why we are thrilled to have Chalamet on our cover as he sets out to open the final, breathtaking installment of Denis Villeneuve’s Dune trilogy. He and our team, led by photographer Aidan Zamiri, fashion editor Taylor McNeill (with whom I was an assistant at this magazine in 2010), and VF global creative director Jennifer Pastore, trekked to Iceland for a multiday shoot to capture his cover story “A Star on Planet Earth.” Everyone involved—including and especially Timothée—approached it more like a film, or maybe a music video, than a typical cover, and there is a spiritual quality that runs throughout the pictures. “I love that being on the edge of a cliff in Iceland,” Timothée tells me, “you get the same feeling as being in Grand Central.”.

Recent findings suggest that timothée also had the idea that I write the cover story myself, and while I was reluctant, I eventually thought, Why not mix it up? He came over to my apartment in early October for a conversation about Dune; his career; the careers of other actors, musicians, and painters; and especially the careers of the New York Knicks. I took away from our meeting that he may be a movie star, sure, but he approaches everything as an artist. The writing process is a humbling one, though—okay, it’s agony—and since filing the cover story, I have come to believe that every editor really should write a feature now and again to make us more understanding of our writers. Perhaps once a year. Consider it a new rule at Vanity Fair.

Sources indicate that timothée and I were both reading Kevin Roose’s The AGI Chronicles when we met up, and he pointed out that the first several chapters of the book might as well have been the source material for Artificial, Luca Guadagnino’s fresh film starring Andrew Garfield and Yura Borisov. The film presents a villain origin story of OpenAI’s cofounders, particularly CEO Sam Altman. It is the natural inheritor to David Fincher and Aaron ­Sorkin’s 2010 film, The Social Network, which similarly helped answer the how-did-we-get-here question for another quite recent era of technology.

Recent findings suggest that in case you missed it, Altman was recently on the cover of Vanity Fair, sitting atop our revived Newly introduced Establishment list. It inspired a torrent of furious reader feedback, including a few death threats. I understand that those messages were rooted in genuine fear of this technology and ire toward its Dr. Frankenstein founders (and me, by extension, for covering them). But reporting on the powerful—whether power is granted by elections or equities or zettaflops of compute—has always been the mandate of this magazine and will continue to be. We’ll keep the movie stars too.
